extracted.intended_audience: students/newcomers to math olympiads interested in proof-based contests
extracted.subtask_description: A concise how-to guide for people with little or no proof/olympiad experience who want to start training for proof-based math contests; covers what to read first, how to write proofs, recommended contests, books, and problem sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audience / scope
rubrics_metrics.description: This page is meant for people who don’t have much past olympiad/proof experience and are looking to get started. If you aren’t interested in proof-based problems yet, then this page is not for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this material only if you want to do proof-based contests; it intentionally excludes non-proof short-answer contest advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow an (unofficial) syllabus for topic coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: I wrote an unofficial syllabus for math olympiads giving some guidance on what topics appear on math olympiads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a syllabus to identify which topics to learn; see the linked syllabus/handouts for concrete topic lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: First reading: study the welcome letter and its worked examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the USAMO invitation 'welcome letter' which includes a few carefully chosen problems, fully written solutions, and practical advice about exam format, time planning, and common mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try the example problems (expect not to solve them all), then compare your solutions to the provided ones to get a sense of contest expectations and correct solution style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof completeness is paramount
rubrics_metrics.description: If you really have a completely correct solution to a problem, it is actually pretty hard to not get full credit. At least ~90% of the time when a student loses points unexpectedly, it's because their proof is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus first on producing a logically complete argument; missing steps or unstated claims are the most common reason for lost points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write solutions clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: You should still try to write your solutions as clearly as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity helps graders verify completeness; consult linked resources ('How to write a solution', 'Remarks on English', 'How to write proofs') for concrete stylistic advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice proof-writing with feedback (do not practice writing in isolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof-writing will become more natural over time as you solve problems; it is counterproductive to try to practice writing in isolation. Best is to have a friend or coach who can check your work and provide suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lack a coach, use the recommended algorithm: write up neatly, look up the problem on AoPS contest index, compare to reputable solutions, edit your writeup, and post on the thread to get feedback (Cunningham’s Law: wrong solutions get exposed quickly). See Section B.1 of the English handout for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use iterative comparison & community feedback algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical three-step algorithm: (1) Write up your solution neatly; (2) Look up the problem on AoPS contest index and compare to reputable users' solutions; (3) Edit and post your solution on the thread to receive feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure catches most substantial errors; posting invites correction and helps improve proof-writing via community critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider USAMTS as beginner-friendly proof contest
rubrics_metrics.description: USAMTS is a free, individual, online contest open to any students in the USA. Problems are chosen to be beginner-friendly with a spectrum of difficulty, you get a full month to work on problems, and you receive feedback on your proofs rather than just a score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use USAMTS to practice slow, careful proof-writing with feedback before attempting time-limited olympiad exams.

rubrics_metrics.name: USEMO as a fall practice contest (IMO-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: USEMO is a free contest run in the fall intended to mimic the USAMO and IMO in format and difficulty; it offers feedback and can serve as 'practice IMO'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat USEMO as a rehearsal for contest-style timing and problem types closer to national/international olympiads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read recommended books and topic primers
rubrics_metrics.description: There are books and excerpts to learn new classes of problems (e.g., Art and Craft of Problem-Solving by Paul Zeitz; EGMO for geometry; Modern Olympiad Number Theory; OTIS Excerpts for inequalities, functional equations, combinatorics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use topic-specific books to learn techniques you won't encounter in short-answer contests; these are suggestions, not guarantees of success. Pick resources appropriate to your current level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work through past problems from reliable archives
rubrics_metrics.description: At some point you need to work through past problems from recent years of contests — think of encountering problems 'in the wild'. AoPS contest index has an extensive archive with community-contributed solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice broadly using archives; recommended contests include Canada national olympiad, EGMO, IMO and IMO Shortlist, USA Team Selection Tests. Maintain a regular practice habit (e.g., check off solved problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recommendations cautiously (they are suggestions, not guarantees)
rubrics_metrics.description: The listed resources and paths are mere suggestions; doing X does not guarantee achieving your goals, and many good resources may be omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt advice to your personal situation; if you want a definitive 'guaranteed to be enough' list for specific target problems, ask more targeted sources.
